# EEG-based assessment of driver trust in automated vehicles

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Tingru Zhang a,1, Jinfeng Yang a,2, Milei Chen a,3, Zetao Li a,4, Jing Zang b,5, Xingda Qu a,\*,6

a Institute of Human Factors and Ergonomics, College of Mechatronics and Control Engineering, Shenzhen University, Shenzhen, China b School of Industrial Engineering, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, USA

## A R T I C L E I N F O

Keywords: Automated vehicles Driver trust Trust assessment EEG features Machine learning

## A B S T R A C T

Effective collaboration between automated vehicles (AVs) and human drivers relies on maintaining an appropriate level of trust. However, real-time assessment of human trust remains a significant challenge. While initial efforts have delved into the potential use of physiological signals, such as skin conductance and heart rate, to evaluate trust, limited attention has been given to the feasibility of assessing trust through electroencephalogram (EEG) signals. This study aimed to address this issue by using EEG signals to objectively assess driver trust towards AVs. A simulated driving experiment was conducted, where driver trust was manipulated by introducing different types of AV malfunctions. Self-reported trust ratings were collected and used to classify driver trust into three levels: low, medium, and high. A total of 420 time- and frequency-domain EEG features were extracted, and nine machine learning algorithms were applied to construct driver trust assessment models. Additionally, to explore the potential of developing cost-effective models with reduced feature inputs, this study developed trust models using features solely from single brain regions: frontal, parietal, occipital, or temporal. The results showed that the best-performing model, utilizing features from the whole brain and employing the Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) algorithm, achieved an accuracy of 88.44% and an F1-score of 78.31%. In comparison, models based on single brain regions did not achieve comparable performance to the comprehensive model. However, the frontal and parietal regions showed important potentials for developing costeffective trust assessment models. This study also performed feature analysis on the best-performing model to identify features highly responsive to changes in trust. The results showed that an increased power of beta waves tended to indicate a lower level of trust in AVs. These findings contribute to our understanding of the neural correlates of trust in AVs and hold practical implications for the development of trust-aware AV technologies capable of adapting and responding to driver’s trust levels effectively.

## 1. Introduction

Automated vehicles (AVs) have the potential to significantly reduce road traffic accidents, enhance traffic efficiency, and decrease fuel consumption (Mousavi, Osman, Lord, Dixon, & Dadashova, 2021; Zhou, Yu, & Qu, 2019). Moreover, they are expected to provide increased mobility for individuals who are unable to drive due to age or disability (Marletto, 2019). Nevertheless, the realization of these benefits faces several pressing challenges. One crucial concern is establishing and calibrating driver trust toward this technology, as trust plays a pivotal role in determining if and how drivers use AVs (Choi & Ji, 2015; Tinga, Petermeijer, de Reus, Jansen, & van Waterschoot, 2023; Zhang et al., 2019, 2021).

Low levels of trust have been reported as a significant factor impeding drivers’ intention to accept AVs (Choi & Ji, 2015; Liu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2019, 2021; Zmud, Sener, & Wagner, 2016). In a national survey conducted by Liu et al. (2023) in the United States, only 1 % of responders said they trusted AVs, while the proportion of distrust response was 44 %. Similarly, two studies conducted with Chinese participants identified distrust as the predominant factor contributing to low intentions of AV usage (Zhang et al., 2019, 2020). On the other hand, overtrust, characterized by excessive trust placed in AVs, can lead to misuse and abuse of the technology. Drivers with an inappropriately high level of trust are less likely to monitor the driving environment or maintain their hands on the steering wheel, as required by level 2 AVs (Banks, Eriksson, O’Donoghue, & Stanton, 2018). Furthermore, overtrust can compromise driver readiness to regain manual control (Korber, ¨ Baseler, & Bengler, 2018), resulting in prolonged reaction time, reduced vehicular control, and increased accident risk (Chu & Liu, 2023; Worle ¨ & Metz, 2023). Several real-world accidents involving AVs have been attributed to overtrust (National Transportation Safety Board, 2017, 2020). Thus, addressing the issue of inappropriate trust levels poses an enduring challenge for AV designers. To ensure the safe introduction of AVs to road traffic, it is critical to develop AVs that can dynamically adapt to drivers’ trust in real-time, and this requires the use of reliable human trust assessment models.

Self-report measures provide the most direct approach to assess trust and represent the most commonly utilized method in trust-related studies (Hergeth, Lorenz, Vilimek, & Krems, 2016; Jian, Bisantz, & Drury, 2000; Zhang et al., 2019). However, self-reported ratings cannot provide continuous measurements, thereby lacking the capability to estimate real-time trust levels. Additionally, they are intrusive and may pose challenges in applied settings. To continuously estimate driver trust in real-time, objective measurements of trust such as drivers’ monitoring behaviors, skin conductance, and heart rate have been explored (Ayoub, Avetisian, Yang, & Zhou, 2023; Yi et al., 2023a, 2023b). There is also evidence suggesting that specific electroencephalogram (EEG) signals are sensitive to human trust (Hopko & Mehta, 2022; Jung, Dong, & Lee, 2019; Seet et al., 2020; Shafiei, Hussein, Muldoon, & Guru, 2018), raising the possibility of developing EEG-based trust assessment models. However, there is still a lack of efforts in utilizing EEG for quantitatively estimating human trust, especially in the context of realistic interactions with AVs. Motivated by filling this research gap, the present study aimed to develop EEG-based trust assessment models by using machine learning algorithms, with drivers’ EEG signals collected during their interactions with simulated automated driving systems with potential malfunctions. Additionally, this study explored single brain region modeling and feature importance analysis, providing a foundation for the development of lightweight and cost-effective systems.

The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

1) This study proposes a trust assessment method based on EEG, distinguishing itself from conventional self-report measures that are subjective in nature and fail to provide real-time feedback. It also contrasts with previous studies that utilized skin conductance, heartrate, and eye-related features for assessing trust levels.

2) The research explores the feasibility of trust modeling based on a single brain region. By concentrating on features from a specific brain region, it enables the use of a cost-effective EEG device with fewer electrodes for trust assessment. This approach also results in a decreased number of features for processing, thereby reducing the computational demands. In essence, this research contributes to the development of lightweight wearable trust assessment systems.

3) This study performs feature analysis on the best-performing trust assessment model, helping to identify features most sensitive to changes in trust. This part of work contributes to an enhanced understanding of the neural mechanisms of trust.

## 2. Related works

Unfortunately, human trust is notoriously hard to measure. According to the well-recognized definition proposed by Lee and See (2004), trust in automation refers to “the attitude that an agent will help achieve an individual’s goals in a situation characterised by uncertainty and vulnerability”. Since trust is a purely psychological construct, self-report measures provide the most direct means of assessing it (Hergeth et al., 2016). To this end, several questionnaires have been proposed, with the 12-item scale developed by Jian et al. (2000) being one of the most widely accepted measures for trust towards general automated systems. More recently, questionnaires specifically designed to assess trust toward AVs have also been developed and validated (Holthausen, Wintersberger, Walker, & Riener, 2020; Zhang et al., 2019). Self-report measures have been commonly used in trust studies (Kohn, De Visser, Wiese, Lee, & Shaw, 2021) due to their intuitive nature, cost-effectiveness, and ease to use. However, self-reports have limitations in that they do not provide continuous measurements and therefore cannot capture real-time fluctuations in trust. Additionally, self-reports are impractical for use in real-world driving scenarios as they are intrusive to primary driving tasks. These limitations restrict the direct application of self-reports in the development of adaptive AVs capable of monitoring and responding to changes in driver trust.

To address the need for deployable measures of driver trust, researchers explored the potential of various continuous and nonintrusive behavioral and physiological features. Driver body postures have been used to quantify trust, as human behaviors tend to be modulated by trust. Yu, Bao, Zhang, Sullivan, and Flannagan (2021) demonstrated that the movement of drivers’ hands across different steering wheel positions was an effective indicator of trust levels. However, Wright, Horrey, Lesch, and Rahman (2016) did not find any significant correlations between self-reported trust levels and driver head, hand, or foot positions. The associations between driver attention allocation patterns and trust levels have also received research attention. Drivers with a higher level of trust tend to have fewer and shorter fixations on the road, while exhibiting more and longer fixations on non-driving related tasks (NDRTs) (Hergeth et al., 2016; Korber ¨ et al., 2018; Petersen, Robert, Yang, & Tilbury, 2019; Walker, Wang, Martens, & Verwey, 2019). Inspired by the advancement of wearable devices for monitoring physiological signals, recent studies have also explored the sensitivity of physiological indicators, such as electrodermal activity (EDA) and heart rate, to changes in driver trust (Akash, Hu, Jain, & Reid, 2018; Ayoub et al., 2023; Morris, Erno, & Pilcher, 2017; Petersen et al., 2019; Walker et al., 2019; Waytz, Heafner, & Epley, 2014). Generally, higher trust has been reported to be associated with lower EDA (Morris et al., 2017; Walker et al., 2019) and attenuated heart rate variations (Waytz et al., 2014).

However, given that these signals function as indirect markers of human cognitive processes, there exists a compelling motivation to investigate more direct metrics for assessing trust. EEG emerges as a promising solution, as it is capable of elucidating specific cognitive state information relevant to trust (Victor, Tivesten, Gustavsson, Johansson, Sangberg, & Ljung, 2018). The high temporal resolution of EEG facilitates the capture of rapid changes in neural activity over short durations, which is crucial for real-time monitoring of dynamic trust. The recent advent of wearable EEG devices enables long-term non-invasive recording of brain signals while individuals are outside the lab and in motion (Casson, 2019; Ferrari, Ismailov, Badier, Greco, & Ismailova, 2020). This technological advancement further presents the potential for the development of applications for real-world trust monitoring.

Preliminary work has revealed various neural correlates of human trust in automation (Hopko & Mehta, 2022; Jung et al., 2019; Seet et al., 2020; Shafiei et al., 2018). Oh, Seong, and Yi (2017) found that the power of alpha and beta waves was stronger, while the power of gamma wave was weaker in trust situations compared to distrust situations. Similarly, Jung et al. (2019) reported that the power of theta wave (6–10 Hz) from the frontal brain region decreased with trust levels. Wang, Hussein, Rojas, Shafi, and Abbass (2018) attempted to quantify the relationship between trust and brain activities by applying a human-AI collaboration game. Their results suggested that among all the investigated brain waves, the power of delta and gamma waves showed the most significant correlations with trust levels. Furthermore, they identified the frontal and occipital areas as the two predominant brain regions sensitive to trust changes. Another study by Seet et al. (2020) demonstrated that the power of alpha wave from the right frontal brain region was the most promising neural measure of trust. Apart from the frequency-domain features of EEG signals mentioned above, timedomain features, such as variance of EEG waves, have been found to be associated with variations in trust (Akash et al., 2018; Jung et al., 2019). Additionally, recent evidence has shown that connectivity patterns among different brain regions and event-related potentials (ERPs) are also sensitive to trust changes (De Visser et al., 2018; Hopko & Mehta, 2022).

The abovementioned studies have revealed significant correlations between behavioral and physiological features and trust levels, providing theoretical groundwork for the development of trust assessment models. Various approaches have been explored in establishing trust models with different features. Yu et al. (2021) employed the random forest algorithm to predict trust, incorporating driver hand position-related features and demographic information such as age and gender as the model inputs. The overall prediction accuracy was approximately 80 %. Yi et al., (2023b) applied typical machine learning algorithms to predict driver trust-change directions during takeover transitions. They considered physiological responses (i.e., skin conductance and heart rate) and takeover factors (e.g., takeover lead time) as input features. The random forest model demonstrated the best performance with an accuracy of 73.7 % and an F1 score of 77.3 %. In their subsequent work (Yi, Cao, Song, Wang, Guo, & Huang, 2023a), the authors introduced a label smoothing-based convolutional neural network to integrate physiological signals and takeover-related features for recognizing drivers’ levels of trust in AVs. The proposed model showed an accuracy of 73.7 % and an F1-score of 75.3 %. Ayoub et al. (2023) employed EDA, heart rate, and eye-related metrics to assess driver trust. The best-performing model achieved an accuracy of 81.6 % and an F1-score of 89.1 %.

There is still a lack of efforts in utilizing EEG for quantitatively estimating human trust. We found only two related studies. In particular, Choo and Nam (2022) proposed a convolutional neural network model that used EEG image features to estimate operator trust when interacting with automation, achieving an estimation accuracy of 94 %. Akash et al. (2018), using EEG and EDA features, proposed a quadratic discriminant classifier to differentiate trust and distrust towards AVs, achieving an average accuracy of 71 %. These two studies support the applicability of EEG features in trust assessment. However, both studies have only required participants to monitor automation failures and respond by pressing key buttons. Such task paradigm is quite different from naturalistic interaction with Level 2 or Level 3 AVs in which drivers not only need to monitor for possible failures but also have to take over the vehicle and drive manually in case of automation failures. Furthermore, both studies have utilized features from the entire brain, which requires significant efforts in terms of recording and computation. The human brain is composed of various regions, each responsible for different functions and processes. The specific roles of different brain regions in trust assessment are still not fully understood. If models built using features from a single brain region can achieve comparable or even superior performance compared to models using the entire brain, it would significantly contribute to the development of real-world trust assessment applications.

From a detailed literature review, it has been identified that there is limited evidence regarding EEG-based driver trust assessment models, particular those derived from realistic interactions with AVs. Additionally, existing studies have not explored the roles of complex brain regions in trust assessment. This study aims to address these research gaps by collecting data from a simulated driving experiment and subsequently developing EEG-based trust assessment models. Concerning the choice of algorithms, the literature has predominantly explored conventional machine learning algorithms, including logistic regression (LR), support vector machine (SVM), quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA), decision tree (DT), K-nearest neighbors (KNN), random forest (RF), and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) (Akash et al., 2018; Ayoub et al., 2023; Yi et al., 2023b; Yu et al., 2021). Two studies have applied convolutional neural network (CNN) to develop trust assessment models, however, their performance did not consistently surpass traditional approaches (Choo & Nam, 2022; Yi et al., 2023a). Furthermore, advanced deep learning models like CNN often require substantial computing resources and extensive amounts of data (Maman et al., 2020), potentially limiting their real-time applicability. Therefore, this study only considered traditional machine learning algorithms to develop trust assessment models. Given that XGBoost has emerged as a robust algorithm for trust modeling (Ayoub et al., 2023), this study seeks to explore whether other boosting classifiers can yield similar or even superior performance. As a result, this study involves the application of conventional machine learning algorithms commonly employed in the literature, coupled with new boosting algorithms, to develop EEG-based trust models.

Fig. 1 provides an overview of the proposed research framework. Specifically, a simulated driving experiment was conducted, during which driver trust levels were maneuvered by introducing different types of AV malfunctions. Both subjective trust ratings and objective EEG signals were recorded. The raw EEG signals were pre-processed, and time-domain and frequency-domain EEG features were extracted. These extracted features were categorized into four distinct brain regions: frontal, temporal, occipital and parietal. Trust models were initially developed using features from the whole brain and subsequently with features isolated from single brain regions utilizing nine classifiers. To identify the best-performing model, the performances of these models were compared using the Friedman test. Finally, the bestperforming model was subjected to a detailed analysis, including a confusion matrix and feature importance assessment, to explore key factors contributing to trust assessment. The findings of this study contribute to a better understanding of the neural correlations of trust. Moreover, the practical implications involve the potential application of these findings in continuous assessment of driver trust, complementing the thriving developments in monitoring of other mental states, such as fatigue and distraction, for future AVs.

This rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 3 provides a description of the driving experiment conducted in this study. Section 4 presents the techniques used for data pre-processing, feature extraction, and feature selection. It also provides a brief introduction to the classifiers utilized in the study. Section 5 shows the performance of the proposed models. Section 6 discusses the implications and limitations of this study. Section 7 presents the conclusions drawn from the research.

## 3. Driving experiment

## 3.1. Participants

A total of 72 college students participated in the driving experiment, with an equal number of males (36) and females (36). The participants had an average age of 22.6 years (SD = 1.6), ranging from 18 to 28 years. All participants held a valid driving license and had normal or corrected-to-normal vision. They were in good health and abstained from drugs and alcohol for 24 h prior to the experiment. The participants were randomly assigned to one of three experimental conditions: normal, miss, or false alarm, with 24 participants (12 males and 12 females) in each condition. There were no significant differences in age or driving experience among the three conditions (age: p = 0.178; driving experience: $p = 0 . 1 4 0 )$

## 3.2. Apparatus

Fig. 2. presents an overview of the driving simulator and EEG-

recording device used in this experiment.

Driving simulator. The driving simulator consisted of three 27-inch LED displays, a high-performance computer, a Logitech steering wheel, brake and accelerator pedals, and a driver’s seat. The simulator was equipped with UC-Win/Road software, which presented various driving scenarios. Driving data such as speed, acceleration, and lane position were recorded at a frequency of 60 Hz. The simulator could operate in either manual or automated mode, and an activation/deactivation button for automated driving was installed on steering wheel.

EEG-recording device. Participant brain waves were recorded using ANT Neuro (ANT-Neuro). It featured 32 scalp channels and recorded brain signals at a frequency of 500 Hz. The electrode placements followed the international 10–20 system. To ensure optimal signal quality, the contact impedance between the electrodes and the participant’s skin was maintained below 20 kΩ.

## 3.3. Experimental design

The experiment employed a between-subjects design with a 2 (gender) × 3 (experiment condition) factorial structure. The three experiment conditions were normal, miss, and false alarm, differed in the way how a take-over request (TOR) was provided in scenario 4. The specific variations among these conditions will be outlined in the subsequent section.

## 3.4. Driving scenario and NDRT

Driving scenario. A two-way 95-km long road, with three lanes in each direction, was created to simulate city driving. Participants were instructed to primarily stay in the middle lane unless dealing with TORs.

A TOR was triggered when the automated driving system was unable to handle a road hazard, requiring control of the vehicle transferred back to the human driver. Eight TOR scenarios (4 types of hazards × 2 levels of road curvatures) were developed. The four types of hazards were broken vehicle, working zone, pedestrian crossing, and landslide, and the two road curvatures were straight roads and sharp curves of 200 m radius.

Fig. 3 provides a visual representation of the detailed arrangements in one scenario. The participants initially drove in automated driving mode, where the system maintained a constant speed of 80 km/h. Participants had the freedom to perform the NDRT at their own pace. In most scenarios, TORs were presented in a standardized format. When the participant’s vehicle was approximately 10 s away from a hazard (approximately 278 m), a TOR was triggered. The TOR consisted of a 75- dB sinusoidal sound (2,010 Hz, duration 0.47 s) and a red text prompt displayed in the lower area of the windshield. This TOR format aligns with the general warning design guidelines proposed by Wogalter, Mayhorn, and Laughery (2021) and has been validated for its effectiveness in alerting drivers to take over control (Hergeth et al., 2016). At the onset of TOR, participants were required to press the X button on the steering wheel to switch to manual driving and handle the impending hazard. After successfully passing the hazard and driving for an additional 1 km, participants were reminded to transfer back to automated driving. Then, after driving for another 1 km, participants were asked to orally provide trust ratings. The trust rating utilized a single-item scale ranging from 0 to 100, based on previous studies (Choo & Nam, 2022; Hergeth et al., 2016; Seet et al., 2020). One scenario concluded after participants had finished providing their trust rating.

TOR in scenario 4 was set differently among three experiment conditions. In the normal condition, TOR was correctly given in response to pedestrian crossing event. In the miss condition, the AV failed to detect the crossing pedestrian hazard, resulting in the absence of a TOR. Participants had to detect and deal with the hazard themselves. In the false alarm group, a TOR was generated despite no pedestrian or any other hazards were presented. It was expected that the two types of malfunctions would induce different levels of trust from the participants.

NDRT: The NDRT used in this study involved a typing task where participants were required to accurately enter Chinese characters displayed on a tablet. This particular NDRT has been extensively utilized in driving studies as a means to replicate visual-manual distractions. For this study, the NDRT was implemented using a Huawei MatePad Pro tablet with a screen size of 10.8 in. The tablet was positioned to the right of the steering wheel, simulating the placement of a center control panel in an actual vehicle. Consequently, participants were required to divert their visual attention completely away from the road when engaging in the NDRT. It is important to note that no feedback regarding task performance was provided to the participants.

## 3.5. Procedure

Upon arrival, participants were briefed on aims and procedures of this experiment. They were then asked to sign the informed consent form. Next, they engaged in a practice session with the NDRT and familiarized themselves with operating the driving simulator. Afterward, participants were equipped with an EEG headset and commenced the formal driving phase. Throughout the experiment, they were instructed to adhere to road traffic laws and TORs. The entire duration of the experiment spanned approximately 60 min.

## 4. Data analysis

## 4.1. Pre-processing

Based on commonly employed pre-processing strategies in prior studies (Li, Yang, & Yan, 2022; Yang, Guan, Ma, & Li, 2019), the following procedures were implemented: (1) a zero-phase finite impulse response (FIR) band pass filter (1–30 Hz) was used to remove noise (Widmann, Schroger, ¨ & Maess, 2015); (2) the raw signals were rereferenced to the average reference; (3) the FASTER toolbox was utilized to identify and flag bad channels, which were subsequently removed using spherical interpolation (Nolan, Whelan, & Reilly, 2010); (4) independent component analysis (ICA) was used to decompose EEG signals, and the ADJUST toolbox was applied to identify and remove artifacts (Mognon, Jovicich, Bruzzone, & Buiatti, 2011).

## 4.2. Trust label and feature extraction

The EEG signals recorded within a distance of 1 km before the trust rating, which corresponds to a duration of approximately 45 s, were used to extract features for model development. The periods were divided into multiple 16-second epochs with 50 % overlap (i.e., a step of 8 s), resulting in approximately 5 epochs extracted for each scenario.

An epoch was labeled as “low trust” if the oral rating fell within the range of [0, 60), “medium trust” if it fell within [60, 80), and “high trust” if it fell within [80, 100]. The classification thresholds were determined by referring to a study (Manchon, Bueno, & Navarro, 2021) reporting that the average trust scores of distrustful and trustful drivers were 60 and 80, respectively, using a 100-point scale rating system. The dataset consisted of 2,239 samples in the high trust group, 458 samples in the medium trust group, and 98 samples in the low trust group.

Six time-domain features were computed from each epoch, including mean, maximum, minimum, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis of EEG waves. To calculate frequency-domain features, EEG waves were first categorized into four bands, namely, delta (1–4 Hz), theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–13 Hz), and beta (13–30 Hz). The amplitude and power spectral density (PSD) of each band were then calculated using Fast Fourier Transformation (FFT) and the Welch algorithm, respectively (Fan et al., 2022). As a result, a total of eight frequency-domain features were obtained (2 features × 4 bands). With six time-domain features and eight frequency-domain features extracted from each of the 30 recording channels, the complete feature set consists of 420 EEG features. The mathematical formulas for feature extraction are shown in Appendix A.

## 4.3. Imbalanced data augmentation and feature selection

The dataset in this study is moderately imbalanced as the minority class (low trust) makes up only 3.5 % of the data. It is argued that such imbalanced dataset is more representative of the real-world problem as low trust may only be induced when malfunctions or accidents occur, which are supposed to be rare events. However, learning from imbalanced data is challenging since traditional algorithms tend to be biased towards the majority class. To overcome this problem, the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) method (Fernandez, ´ Garcia, Herrera, & Chawla, 2018) was applied to augment the minority classes in the training set. Further, to identify the most relevant features for building a trust model, the Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) method combined with the Logistic Regression model was used for feature selection. The F1-score metric was utilized to determine the optimal number of features for the model. The basic pseudocodes for feature selection are showed in Algorithm 1.

**Algorithm 1. Feature selection.**

## Input:

(X\_train, Y\_train) and (X\_test, Y\_test)//Data set is divided into two sets, including 70% of the training set and 30% of the testing set **Output:** Best Feature Subset :fs\_train , fs\_test **Steps:** 1: Initial fs\_train , fs\_test and bestF1 as empty 2: **for** each Features subset in maxFeatures **do** 3: rfe ← RFE.fit(train\_X, train\_Y) 4: train\_X\_New ← rfe.transform(train\_X) 5: test\_Y\_New ← rfe.transform(test\_X) 6: LR.fit(train\_X\_New, train\_Y) # Train the model 7: y\_pred = LR.predict(test\_Y\_New) # Predict on the test set 8: f1 = f1\_score(test\_Y, y\_pred,) # Calculate F1 score for each feature subset 9: **if** f1 score > bestF1 **then** 10: fs\_train = train\_X\_New, fs\_test = test\_X\_New 11: **end for** 12: **return** fs\_train,fs\_test

## 4.4. Classifier overview

Samples were apportioned into training and test sets, with a 70–30 split. To build trust assessment models, nine classifiers were employed: DT, KNN, SVM, RF, adaptive boosting (AdaBoost), gradient boosting decision tree (GBDT), XGBoost, light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM), and multilayer perceptron (MLP).

DT, KNN, and SVM are well-known algorithms commonly used for classification problems. RF operates by creating multiple decision trees and each decision tree is built on independently drawn samples (Li & Chen, 2020). After generating numbers of trees, the final decision class is based on a vote. RF is considered as one of the best classifiers for its robustness to multicollinearity, missing data, and unbalanced data problems (Li & Chen, 2020). In addition, RF can well predict the role of up to thousands of explanatory variables (Li & Chen, 2020).

Adaboost is a type of boosting algorithms. Boosting is a class of machine learning methods based on the idea that a combination of simple classifiers can perform better than any of the sample classifiers alone (Ferreira & Figueiredo, 2012). Boosting algorithms can iteratively adjust weights of the training set samples and weights of the base learning algorithms to improve system accuracy. AdaBoost, XGBoost, GBDT, and LightGBM are the four widest-used boosting algorithms. The key idea behind AdaBoost is to use weighted versions of the same training data instead of randomly subsamples thereof. Given that the same training data are repeatedly used, this classifier does not require very large of sample size. It uses the error of previous simple classifier to update the sample weight.

GBDT differs from Adaboost in that it is based on gradient descent, where the base classifiers are trained in the direction of the negative gradient of the loss function. As a result, each time a new base classifier is added, the loss function is reduced, resulting in the best integrated model (Li & Chen, 2020). It has a strongly generalizing ability and is robust to overfitting. XGBoost is proposed by Chen and Guestrin (2016) based on GBDT framework. It differs from GBDT in that it introduces the regularization term in the loss function and adopts a second-order Taylor series as the objective function, which can further tackle overfitting problems (Li & Chen, 2020). LightGBM is also developed by referring to GBDT framework (Ke et al., 2017). It aims to improve computational efficiency so that big data predictions can be solved more effectively. Specifically, it uses histogram-based algorithms and leafwise growth strategies to increase training speed and reduce memory consumption.

MLP is a type of neural networks that consists of three types of layers: input layer, output layer, and hidden layer. The input layer receives input signals to be processed while the output layer exports classification results. An arbitrary number of hidden layers placed in between the input and output layers are the computational engine of MPL. In MPL, data flow in forward direction while neurons are trained with backpropagation algorithms (Gardner & Dorling, 1998). MPL has been widely used for EEG signal classification (Lotte, Congedo, Lécuyer, Lamarche, & Arnaldi, 2007). Detailed information, including the mathematical models associated with these classifiers, can be found in Kubat and Kubat (2017).

We engaged in hyperparameter tuning for each of these algorithms using a grid search, adhering to the specific values and ranges indicated in Appendix B. This phase entails fitting the model to the training data through various hyperparameter combinations and selecting the combination that yields the best results on the validation set.

## 4.5. Performance evaluation metrics

To comprehensively evaluate model performance in the case of an imbalanced multiclass classification problem, four metrics derived from the confusion matrix, namely accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, were calculated. The four metrics are formulated as:

$$
\text {Accuracy} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \frac {a _ {i i}}{\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {k} a _ {i j}}\tag{1}
$$

$$
\text {Precision} = \frac {1}{k} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \left(a _ {i i} / \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {k} a _ {i j}\right)\tag{2}
$$

$$
\text {Recall} = \frac {1}{k} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \left(a _ {i i} / \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {k} a _ {j i}\right)\tag{3}
$$

$$
\text {F1} - \text {score} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {k} \frac {2 * \text {Precision} (i) * \text {Recall} (i)}{\text {Precision} (i) + \text {Recall} (i)}\tag{4}
$$

where $\mathrm { a _ { i j } ,   i , j \in [ 1 , k ] }$ are cells of a k × k multi-class confusion matrix and indicate frequencies of samples with true class $\mathbf { C _ { i } }$ and predictive class $\mathbf { C _ { j } } .$

When identifying the best model, F1-score was used as the main performance measure since it is a harmonic mean of precision and recall, and better than accuracy when the data is imbalanced for classification analysis (Ayoub et al., 2023). For the identified best-performing model, two additional evaluations were performed. First, confusion matrix was examined to evaluate its performance in the minority class. Second, the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method (Lundberg & Lee, 2017) was employed to rank the features based on their importance, which helps identify the most influential features in the trust assessment.

## 5. Results

## 5.1. Trust assessment models based on the whole brain

Using RFE method, a total of 300 features were selected from the whole brain region feature set to develop trust assessment models. The results, as presented in Table 1, showed that the LightGBM model achieved the highest accuracy (88.44 %), precision (81.19 %), and F1-score (78.31 %), indicating its superiority in capturing trust patterns. The GBDT model achieved the second-highest accuracy (87.82 %) and F1- score (78.21 %). The precision and recall of the GBDT model were also above 75 %, suggesting this was also an effective trust assessment model. Conversely, the DT and AdaBoost models demonstrated the poorest performance in trust assessment, with an F1-score of 50.08 % and 55.29 %, respectively.

## 5.2. Trust assessment models based on a single brain region

Using features from a single brain region to build trust assessment models offers potential advantages in terms of cost-effectiveness and time efficiency. The placement of the 32 electrodes in this study and their associations with the 4 brain regions are depicted in Fig. 4. The RFE method selected $7 4 , 7 2 ,$ 40 and 86 features from the frontal, temporal, occipital and parietal regions, respectively. The selected features from each brain region were utilized to develop trust models with the 9 classifiers. The performance of each model on the four metrics are listed in the Appendix C.

Fig. 5 presents the best models, i.e., models with the highest F1- score, achieved by each brain region and their performance on the four metrics. The results suggested that LightGBM delivered the best when using features from the frontal, temporal, and occipital regions, while RF showed the highest performance with features from the parietal region. Notably, the frontal and parietal regions demonstrated superior performance compared to the temporal and occipital regions.

## 5.3. Comparing brain region performance in trust modeling

Fig. 6 shows the averaged performance across the nine classifiers for both the whole brain and the four single brain regions. Friedman test was conducted to statistically compare the performance of different brain regions. The results indicated that the effects of brain regions on accuracy $\mathrm{F}(4,40)=30.49,p<0.001$ , precision $\mathrm{F}(4,40)=27.39,p<$ 0.001), recall $\mathrm{F}(4,40)=22.31,\ p<0.001$ , and F1-score $\left( \mathrm{F}(4,40) = \right.$ $2 8 . 0 9 , p < 0 . 0 0 1 )$ were all found to be significant. Pairwise comparisons (Fig. 6) revealed the whole brain in general exhibited significantly better performance compared to the single brain regions. For instance, the F1- score of the whole brain was significantly higher than that of the frontal $( p = 0 . 0 1 7 )$ , temporal $( p = 0 . 0 0 3 )$ , occipital $( p < 0 . 0 0 1 )$ , and parietal (p = 0.037) regions. The frontal and parietal brain regions showed significantly superior performance than the occipital region in all four metrics. The frontal region outperformed the temporal region in accuracy (p = 0.044).

## 5.4. Confusion matrix and feature importance analysis

According to the aforementioned results, the LightGBM model using whole brain features emerged as the top-performing model. In this section, a more comprehensive analysis of this model was performed.

First, the confusion matrix of this model was derived (Fig. 7). The results indicated that the model effectively learned the classification boundary between the low and medium trust, as well as that between the low and high trust, supporting its effectiveness in distinguishing low trust from medium and high trust. However, the model exhibited some challenges in accurately distinguishing between medium trust and high trust.

Then, feature importance values were calculated using the SHAP method. Fig. 8 presents the top 10 features that contributed the most to the model. Interestingly, eight of them were PSD features, with five from beta waves and three from delta waves, indicating the critical roles of the PSD of beta wave in trust assessment. From a brain region perspective, the majority of the 10 features belonged to the parietal region (i.e., C3\_PSD\_Beta, CP2\_PSD\_Beta, Cz\_PSD\_Delta, Pz\_PSD\_Delta, FC1\_Skew, FC5\_PSD\_Delta).

Fig. 9 presents the SHAP summary plots, displaying the specific impacts of important features in each trust class. The plot can be interpreted as follows: 1) the color of each dot represents the value of the corresponding feature, with blue indicating smaller values and red indicating larger values. 2) The horizontal position of each dot represents the magnitude of the SHAP value. Dots positioned farther to the right indicate a larger positive contribution, while dots located farther to the left indicate a larger negative contribution.

An inspection of Fig. 9 showed that CP2\_PSD\_Beta showed the most profound impact on high trust identification, with a smaller value associated with a higher probability of being classified as high trust. C3\_PSD\_Beta contributed the most in medium trust identification, with a smaller value associated with a higher probability of being classified as medium trust. CP5\_PSD\_Beta was the most important feature for low trust identification, but a smaller value reduced the possibility of being classified as low trust. It was also worth noting that the magnitudes of the SHAP values in medium trust were relatively smaller compared to those in high and low trust, suggesting that the features might be less confirmative in identifying medium trust. This may explain why medium trust tended to be mistakenly classified as high trust.

## 6. Discussion

This study aimed to develop trust assessment models using EEG features. In a simulated driving experiment, driver trust was manipulated by introducing different types of AV malfunctions. Self-reported trust ratings were collected and used to classify driver trust into three levels: low, medium, and high. A total of 420 time- and frequencydomain EEG features were extracted, and nine machine learning algorithms were applied to construct driver trust assessment models. Additionally, this study explored the potential of developing low-cost models with features from single brain regions.

One significant contribution of this study lies in the compelling evidence it provides for the feasibility of using EEG features to predict driver trust. The best-performing model in this study utilized LightGBM and incorporated features from the whole brain. This best model achieved an accuracy of 88.44 % and an F1-score of 78.31 %. In related literature, three similar studies also utilized physiological data to develop models for assessing driver trust (Akash et al., 2018; Ayoub et al., 2023; Yi et al., 2023b). In particular, Yi et al., (2023b) combined EDA, heart rate, and driving features to predict trust change directions, achieving an accuracy of 73.7 % and an F1-score of 77.3 %. Akash et al. (2018) focused on EEG and EDA features to predict driver trust, reporting a mean accuracy of 73.13 % and a recall of 65.35 %. Ayoub et al. (2023) used EDA, heart rate, and eye features to distinguish trust and distrust, with the best model achieving an accuracy of 81.6 % and an F1-score of 89.1 %. Directly comparing these results to the findings of this study can be challenging due to variations in experimental paradigms, trust labeling approaches, trust groups, and features used. Nevertheless, based on the available information, it can be argued that the model developed in this study demonstrated comparable or even superior performance to the state-of-the-art trust classification models reported in the literature, especially considering that this study classified trust into three levels instead of adopting a binary classification as used in previous studies.

Another contribution is that this study developed trust models that utilized features from single brain regions, which highlighted the potential for creating cost-effective models with a reduced number of features. The results indicated that while the single-brain-region models did not outperform the whole-brain model, the frontal and parietal regions showed promise for constructing lightweight models. In comparison to the whole-brain model’s 88.44 % accuracy, the frontal and parietal regions achieved 87.72 % and 86.89 %, respectively, with differences of less than 2 %. Similarly, compared to the whole-brain model’s F1 score of 78.31 %, the F1 scores for the frontal and parietal regions were 75.25 % and 74.54 %, respectively, with differences within 4 %. In the field of neuroscience, the frontal region is well-known for its vital role in executive functions, including planning, decision-making, and the integration of emotional and cognitive signals during trust judgments (Bellucci, Molter, & Park, 2019). This crucial role in trust assessment has been empirically supported by studies in the context of AVs. For instance, Seet et al. (2020) observed that alpha power from the frontal region was sensitive to decrease in self-reported trust in AVs resulting from malfunctions. Additionally, Wang et al. (2018) identified the frontal area as a predominant brain region correlated with trust in automation. On the other hand, the relationship between parietal region and trust has received less investigation in the literature. By demonstrating that models built using features from the parietal region can achieve competitive performance, this study suggests that the parietal region may hold potential as a neural measure for assessing trust.

Lastly, a feature importance analysis was conducted on the bestperforming model. One notable category of features that holds particular relevance for trust assessment is the PSD of beta waves, especially recorded from channels CP5, C3, CP2, Fp1, and Pz. Specifically, an elevated power of beta waves tends to signify a lower level of trust in AVs. Previous studies have suggested that increased beta power may be linked to heightened cognitive processing or be indicative of an anxious state (Li et al., 2023; Peng et al., 2022). Collectively, it is plausible that drivers with lower trust may allocate more attentional resources to monitoring the status of AVs or may experience greater uncertainty or anxiety concerning $\mathbf { A } \mathbf { V } \mathbf { s } ,$ thereby exhibiting higher beta power. Moreover, in line with previous research highlighting the effectiveness of LightGBM in handling imbalanced data (Abenna, Nahid, Bouyghf, & Ouacha, 2022; Khoshgoftaar, Golawala, & Van Hulse, 2007; Li & Chen, 2020), this study confirmed its superior performance when compared to other algorithms like DT, SVM, and KNN in trust assessment.

In practical terms, these findings hold significant implications for the development of trust-aware AV systems. A trust-aware AV should possess the capability to adapt to changes in human trust levels in realtime, fostering a dynamic and adaptive human-AV relationship. Achieving this goal involves addressing three key issues: defining an appropriate trust level, identifying effective countermeasures for adjusting trust levels, and conducting real-time assessments of trust levels (Ayoub et al., 2023). This study, which achieved a higher level of accuracy and F1 score for EEG-based trust assessment, presents valuable solutions to the third issue. Furthermore, the exploration of models based on specific brain regions underscores the potential for costeffective solutions, as these models require fewer electrodes for the EEG device and demand fewer computing resources for the processor. In addition, the identification of the crucial role of PSD related features holds significant practical implications since PSD features are computationally efficient (Xiong, Zhang, Wang, & Gu, 2020), enabling realtime trust assessment using wearable devices in AVs. Moreover, existing literature suggests that modeling with the most influential features can yield performance comparable to, or even surpassing models that incorporate all features (Zhou et al., 2020). Consequently, future studies may develop lightweight trust assessment models with only these identified top features. These contributions are particularly strengthened by the advent of wearable EEG devices (Casson, 2019), which enable long-term, non-invasive recording of brain signals beyond the constraints of a lab environment.

This study has certain limitations and areas for future exploration. Firstly, the models developed in this research were constructed based on generalized data from all participants. However, EEG signals are known to exhibit non-stationary and non-linear characteristics, along with significant inter-individual variability. Therefore, future research efforts may explore the potential benefits of personalized models or generalized models that can adapt to individual differences over time. Secondly, the experiments conducted in this study took place within a simulated driving environment, which may not fully replicate real-world driving scenarios. It would be valuable for future studies to validate our findings using data collected from real-road testing to ensure the generalizability of the trust assessment models. Lastly, this study utilized a medicalgrade EEG device, which facilitated the accurate identification of brain signals associated with trust in AVs. However, such devices are costly and may have limited practical wearability. Future research efforts could investigate the feasibility of utilizing portable and costeffective EEG devices to capture these signals while achieving comparable or even improved levels of accuracy. This exploration could contribute to the development of more practical trust assessment solutions.

## 7. Conclusions

Assessing driver trust poses a significant challenge in the development of adaptive AVs. Traditional subjective evaluation methods, prevalent in the majority of trust-related studies, suffer from discontinuity and a lack of real-time measurement capabilities. In recent years, some studies have explored trust assessment methods based on behavioral signals or physiological signals such as EDA (Ayoub et al., 2023; Yi et al., 2023a, 2023b). However, these signals serve as indirect indicators of trust. EEG, on the other hand, directly measures brain electrical activity, offering a more direct reflection of neural processes associated with trust. Additionally, the high temporal resolution of EEG, capable of capturing rapid changes in neural activity over very short durations, proves crucial for real-time monitoring of dynamic trust variations in human-AV interaction.

This study represents a preliminary effort in developing trust assessment models based on large-scale EEG signals. The bestperformance model, utilizing features subject to the whole brain and employing the LightGBM algorithm, achieved an accuracy of 88.44 % and an F1-score of 78.31 %. These results provide compelling evidence supporting the feasibility of using EEG features to predict driver trust. Moreover, models constructed with features solely from the frontal or parietal regions showed competitive performance, underscoring the potential for developing cost-effective models with a reduced number of features. This study also performed feature analysis on the bestperforming model to identify features highly responsive to changes in trust. The results showed that an increased power of beta waves tended to indicate a lower level of trust in AVs.

These findings offer compelling evidence supporting the feasibility of utilizing EEG features to predict driver trust and advance our understanding of the neural correlates of trust in AVs. Additionally, they carry practical implications for the design and implementation of trust-aware AV systems, while also highlighting directions for the development of lightweight trust assessment models.

## Appendix A

The six time-domain features, which include the mean, maximum, minimum, standard deviation, skewness, and kurtosis of the EEG waves, are computed using the following formula:

(1) Mean

$$
\overline {{X}} = \frac {\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} X _ {i}}{N}\tag{1}
$$

(2) Maximum

$$
X _ {\max} = \max \left\{X _ {1}, X _ {2}, \dots , X _ {N} \right\}\tag{2}
$$

(3) Minimum

$$
X _ {\min} = \min \{X _ {1}, X _ {2},..., X _ {N} \}\tag{3}
$$

(4) Standard deviation

$$
\sigma_ {X} = \sqrt {\frac {\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} \left(X _ {i} - \bar {X}\right) ^ {2}}{N - 1}}\tag{4}
$$

(5) Skewness

$$
\text {Skew} = E \left[ \left(\frac {X - \overline {{X}}}{\sigma_ {X}}\right) ^ {3} \right]\tag{5}
$$

(6) Kurtosis

$$
\text {Kurt} = E \left[ \left(\frac {X - \overline {{X}}}{\sigma_ {X}}\right) ^ {4} \right]\tag{6}
$$

where X<sub>i</sub> represents the raw EEG signal, and N is the signal length.

To calculate frequency-domain features, EEG waves were first categorized into four bands, namely, delta (1–4 Hz), theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–13 Hz), and beta (13–30 Hz). The amplitude and power spectral density (PSD) of each band were then calculated using the following formula:

(7) PSD

$$
P S D (f) = \frac {1}{N} \left| \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {N - 1} x [ n ] e ^ {- j 2 \pi f n T} \right| ^ {2}\tag{7}
$$

(8) Amplitude

$$
A (f) = \left| \sum_ {n = 0} ^ {N - 1} x (n) \cdot e ^ {- \frac {2 n f}{N} f n} \right|\tag{8}
$$

where f is the frequency, N is the length of the sub segment, $x [ n ]$ is the value of the signal at time n, and T is the sampling interval.
